Visuomotor Grasping with World Models
for Surgical Robots
Hongbin Lin, Bin Li, and Kwok Wai Samuel Au
DOI: 10.1177/ToBeAssigned
our policy achieves a 65% success rate in both settings

This work is an extended version of previously published
conference papers [10; 9].

In contrast, our approach learns a single visuomotor
controller that is capable of handling diverse grasping tasks.

Our goal is to control a robotic arm with an arbitrary gripper
to grasp an arbitrary target object within a workspace via a
learned visuomotor policy π that maps temporal observation
to an action command. The size of the gripper and the
target object is within a ball with a diameter of 5cm. The
initial poses of the target object and the robot gripper are
set randomly within the workspace. Visual observations are
captured using an endoscopic stereo camera.

The first four elements of the action vector control the
Cartesian translation of the gripper along thex, y, and z axes,
as well as its Cartesian orientation along the z-axis. These
elements represent delta action commands, constrained by
the maximum translational and rotational magnitudes, ∆xyz
and ∆θ, respectively.

a positive value actuates the
gripper to open, and a non-negative value actuates it to close.

If
the jaws are opened, it closes the jaw with a robot command
[0, 0, 0, 0, −1]. Otherwise, if the jaws are closed, it opens the
jaw with a robot command [0, 0, 0, 0, 1].

When the gripper’s desired position lies outside
the defined workspace, the system actuates the gripper to the
nearest feasible point within the workspace boundary.

We assume that i) the joint positions of the robot arm remain
within the robot’s joint limits throughout the task; ii) both
the target objects and the gripper may be partially occluded,
but are never fully occluded; and iii) the poses of the target
objects and the gripper cannot be tracked explicitly using the
robot’s kinematics or through camera observations.

ssys1 encodes the ID of our task-level states in our
FSM; ssys2 encodes the joint position of the gripper’s jaw;
and ssys3 encodes ID of sub-policies in our hybrid control
architecture

Our visuomotor policy is learned with a world-model-based
algorithm, DreamerV2 [51]. DreamerV2 builds a generative
world model that captures the dynamics of POMDP. The
world model is learned with past ground-truth experiences
sampled from a replay buffer. A visuomotor policy is learned
from generative transitions from the world model with an
actor-critic algorithm. The robot agent generates ground-
truth trajectories by interacting with the environment. The
resulting ground-truth transitions are then stored in the replay
buffer for off-policy learning.

For world models, observation is encoded to a stochastic
latent state z through a Variational Auto-Encoder (V AE)
[58]. Then, the sequences of the latent states are predicted
by Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) [59], a sequence
model with a deterministic recurrent state h. Finally, the
reward, the discount factor, and reconstructive observation
ˆo are predicted based on the encoded hidden state, which
is formed by the concatenation of these states as s = [h, z].

A prior hidden without accessing current observation is
given by ˆs = [h, ˆz], where ˆzt is the estimated stochastic
hidden state predicted by the transition predictor of RSSM
ˆz ∼ pϕ(ˆz|h).

The actor network learns a distribution of actions for each
latent model state, aiming to maximize the cumulative future
task rewards. Meanwhile, the critic network is trained using
temporal difference learning to predict the total future task
rewards [60].

We first estimate the depth and object masks based
on the stereo images. Then we re-project the depth and mask
to images using orthogonal projection. Finally, we use a novel
image representation for the visuomotor’s input image.

The pixel correspondence
and disparity are estimated by a state-of-the-art (SOTA) pre-
trained stereo matching network, IGEV [64]

To overcome these challenges, we utilize a semi-
supervised VOS method, Track Anything Model (TAM)
[65], combining two SOTA pre-trained models, Segment-
Anything Model (SAM) [69] and XMem [70].

Given the annotation, XMem
automatically tracks object masks for the remaining
frames by leveraging both temporal and spatial
correspondence of streaming input images.

a user annotates the
masks for the first frame of the temporal RGB images
in a rollout. With SAM, fine masks can be created
via a few point prompts—approximately two clicks
per object mask.

we
employ a voxel-based orthogonal projection method [73] to
reproject both depth images and segmentation masks into
an equivariant form with respect to the translation of task
objects.

The encoded image consists of three layers
(channels): the first encodes the orthogonal depths, the
second encodes the orthogonal mask, and the third encodes
the system states.

our recurrent RL
policy performs poorly at the beginning of a rollout. This is
primarily due to the fact that the world model of DreamerV2
starts from a blank state [5; 51] at the beginning of each
rollout, resulting in a large estimation error for the latent
states of the world model.

we propose a hybrid
control architecture that combines traditional PID control,
our previously proposed control of virtual clutch (VC) [9],
and our RL policy.

We identify three phases
for a trajectory: i) beginning phase , ii) PID phase , and
iii) RL phase . For the beginning phase, our visuomotor
controller do not observe enough temporal observations.
We identify transitions with the timesteps t < Hbegin in
such a phase

We
employ an idle action that keeps the robot’s joint positions
unchanged.

For the RL phase, the output of our learned visuomotor
policy is directly used for the control command. We use two
hyper-parameters αxyz , αθ ∈ (0, 1] to shrink the magnitudes
of the actuated robot command for discrete action.

If the difference in
z-coordinates between the gripper and the target object
c1z − c2z becomes smaller than a predefined safe threshold,
Zsaf e, after the gripper is actuated by our hybrid-architecture
controller, an additional corrective move is triggered.

the z-axis—by 30mm. This method ensures that the gripper
maintains a certain height relative to the target object. Since
the platform is typically positioned below the target, the
minimum height of the gripper relative to the platform is
greater than or equal to Zsaf e, thus preventing the gripper
from applying excessive force to the platform’s tissue. We
apply this method in our real-robot experiments.

depth images and segmentation masks from the camera are
also directly rendered in simulation, thereby we do not need
to apply depth estimation (in Section 4.3.1) and segmentation
(in Section 4.3.2) in simulation.

For simulation, we use the same experiment setup in our
training scene, except for using different random seeds.

The robotic arms are controlled by an open-source
control system, da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) [78]. Stereo
images are captured by the endoscopic stereo camera with
1080p resolution. The images are center cropped to the size
of 600 × 600 for the controller’s observation.

When the gripper closes, the task is considered complete, and
the gripper is then lifted by 30 mm. If the gripper is holding
an object after being lifted, the FSM state is labeled as the
successful termination. Otherwise, it is labeled as the failed
termination.

capability_assessments.rationale: The paper documents its executed learned recurrent model, actor–critic learning from generated transitions, and control outcomes. L4 does not imply separately reported L1/L2 fidelity, matched L3 alternatives, online MPC, causal identification, or clinical readiness. Underreported action-dependent equations remain a review issue rather than being filled from the cited algorithm.

gate_assessments.rationale: Source/transform descriptions do not establish retained variable-level provenance, availability semantics, and leakage audits.
Implemented learned transitions exist, but future-state/reference prediction evaluation is unreported.
Imagination depth/protocol, drift curves, tolerances, and effective predictive horizon are unreported. The 80-step episode cap is not predictive-horizon validation.
The selected feasibility claim is not a probabilistic coverage guarantee or uncertainty-dependent decision-assurance claim. Stochasticity does not establish either.
Base increments, consistent jaw mapping, complete action-dependent transition semantics, specified-action forecasts, and support remain unresolved.
The reviewed control-feasibility claim does not interpret model outputs as a defined therapeutic intervention effect. This is not a causal-validity endorsement.
Model-coupled policy and control outcomes exist; action coverage and exploitation-specific assessment are incomplete.
Workspace restriction, startup fallback, and reactive height correction lack hazard-specific validation. Zsafe, force/injury outcomes, and comprehensive failure responses are unreported.
Transfer/shift tests exist, but independent specimen/platform replication, overlap controls, and a supported transfer envelope are unresolved.
Physical execution is reported; matched sim-to-real agreement is partial and lacks acceptance criteria. Annotation is not expert output/use evaluation.
The selected claim is preclinical control feasibility, not measured live clinical/workflow benefit.
No operational release decision or authorization is asserted. Such release would require currently unreported governance, monitoring, and change control.

legacy_cells.AM: Dynamic Spotlight Adaptation encodes orthogonally projected depth, masks, and system states as three channels stacked into a 64 × 64 × 3 image
legacy_cells.AT: RSSM uses deterministic recurrent state h and stochastic latent z; a prior predicts z from h without the current observation
legacy_cells.BD: Nine discrete actions: ±x, ±y, ±z translation, ±z rotation, and jaw toggle; normalized five-element command in [−1, 1]
legacy_cells.BF: Workspace-boundary clamping; normalized action clipping; safe-control correction moves gripper upward by 30 mm when vertical clearance is below threshold
legacy_cells.BS: Predicted reward, discount factor, and reconstructed observation
legacy_cells.BT: Actor action-distribution head and critic value head
legacy_cells.BU: Predicted reward; sparse task rewards are +1 for successful termination, −0.1 for failed termination, −0.01 for abnormal progress, and −0.001 for normal progress
legacy_cells.BV: Jointly optimize world model and actor-critic; actor maximizes cumulative future discounted task rewards; critic trained with temporal-difference learning
legacy_cells.EC: Reported control/task success: simulation average success rate 54.1% and grasping score 30.9%; real-robot square phantom study weighted success rate 75%; ex vivo 20 mm needle success rate 65%
legacy_cells.ED: Authors compare simulation and real-robot task success; simulation average success rate 54.1% (Table 2) and square-phantom study weighted success rate 75% (Table 4); these are not identical aggregate test conditions
legacy_cells.EG: Training: 1.1 million timesteps; 6 days per baseline on 4 Nvidia RTX 3090 GPUs and a 16-core CPU. Real-robot controller ran at approximately 1 Hz on an Nvidia TITAN RTX 24 GB GPU and 8-core CPU
legacy_cells.EI: Simulation average success rate: GASv2 54.1%, DreamerV2 0.7%, PPO 0.0%, GASv1 0.1%
legacy_cells.EJ: World-model baselines in simulation: DreamerV2 0.7% average success rate; GASv1 0.1%
legacy_cells.EK: Simulation ablations: GASv2-RawVR 3.4%, GASv2-NoClutch 55.7%, GASv2-NoPID 34.4% average success rate; real-robot GASv2-NoDR showed a reported 47.5% performance drop
legacy_cells.EL: Ex vivo porcine-tissue grasping had 55% success rate; authors report segmentation difficulty because tissue appearance resembles the background, and significant background changes require mask re-annotation
legacy_cells.EM: Hybrid safety control: idle action holds the robot stationary while temporal observations accumulate; PID approach, workspace checks, virtual clutch, and a height-threshold correction move the gripper upward 30 mm to avoid platform contact
legacy_cells.FB: Learned stochastic/deterministic RSSM latent state [h,z], supplemented by explicit FSM, gripper, and controller states; compact DSA image carries depth and object-mask structure
legacy_cells.FL: Stereo perception estimates depth with IGEV and tracks masks with TAM; voxel orthogonal projection and DSA create compact observations; DreamerV2 VAE/RSSM encodes latent state and predicts transitions, reward, discount, and observation; actor-critic learns a visuomotor policy, combined with PID/virtual-clutch/safe-control subpolicies.
legacy_cells.FM: Authors contribute a simulation-trained, object-agnostic surgical grasping policy transferred to phantom and ex vivo scenes; DSA image representation; stereo depth and video-mask perception; hybrid PID/virtual-clutch/RL control; and evaluation on novel objects, grippers, and disturbances.
legacy_cells.FN: Authors report 65% success in phantom-based and ex vivo settings; simulation average success rate 54.1%; square-phantom weighted rate 75%; ex vivo standard-needle rate 65%; controller ran at approximately 1 Hz.
legacy_cells.FO: Authors state that significant background changes require users to re-annotate object masks and that the controller's approximately 1 Hz control frequency limits grasping speed.
legacy_cells.FP: Authors propose investigating unsupervised video-object-segmentation methods to reduce manual annotation and high-frequency control techniques.
legacy_cells.FQ: Authors identify gaps in sim-to-real transfer to ex vivo surgical scenes, stereo-only visuomotor learning for standard RAS setups, and object-agnostic grasping across unseen surgical objects without retraining.
legacy_cells.FR: Evidence is simulation and research-robot testing on phantoms and ex vivo porcine stomach, not prospective in-vivo patient care or clinical benefit. Reported grasp success does not establish patient safety, clinical utility, or identified treatment effects; the authors also report approximately 1 Hz control and annotation dependence under background changes.
